title: The Presumption of Regularity
hook: Courts normally start by assuming the government followed its own rules and told the truth. That default is quiet, load-bearing — and, judges are now saying out loud, forfeitable.
key_points: The presumption of regularity tells judges to assume officials acted in good faith and by the rules unless a challenger proves otherwise.
It exists because courts cannot re-audit every government action; it also sets a high bar for anyone contesting one.
ProPublica identified hundreds of cases since 2025 in which judges criticized Justice Department conduct, and more than 40 that explicitly invoked the presumption.
Judge Paula Xinis told government lawyers: 'You have taken the presumption of regularity, and you've destroyed it.'
Judge Christine O'Hearn said she would 'no longer blindly accept statements of fact' from the government unless made under oath.
Criticism came from judges appointed by presidents of both parties, including Trump appointees in Rhode Island and Indiana.
content_html: Most of what courts do rests on assumptions nobody argues about. One of the quietest is the presumption of regularity: unless a challenger shows otherwise, a judge assumes the government followed its own procedures and acted in good faith. It is a practical necessity — no court could re-audit every federal action — and it puts a heavy burden on anyone claiming an agency broke its own rules. ProPublica reports that federal judges have begun withdrawing it.
extra_html:
Reviewing filings since the start of the current administration, ProPublica found hundreds of cases in which judges criticized Justice Department conduct, and more than 40 that referenced the presumption of regularity explicitly — a doctrine that historically almost never came up. The quotations are unusually direct for judicial writing. Judge Paula Xinis, in litigation over the deportation of a US citizen, told the government: "You have taken the presumption of regularity, and you've destroyed it." Judge Christine O'Hearn wrote that her court would "no longer blindly accept statements of fact from [the U.S. government] unless made under oath." In Minnesota, Judge Patrick J. Schiltz condemned what he called spurious claims and use of the grand jury process against political opponents. Notably, the criticism is not partisan in origin: Trump-appointed judges in Rhode Island and Indiana are among those cited, and former Judge John E. Jones, a Bush appointee, told ProPublica he did not think the annals of the department had ever seen anything close to it.

The consequences compound. Once a judge requires sworn testimony instead of accepting a lawyer's representation, ordinary litigation gets slower and the government loses more often; ProPublica also documents disciplinary referrals of department lawyers and an exodus of veteran attorneys. The general civics point outlasts this particular fight: institutional trust functions as legal infrastructure. When it is spent, nothing formally changes in the statute books, and yet the government's day-to-day advantage in court quietly disappears.

related.title: The Rule of Law
related.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

flashcards.prompt: What is the presumption of regularity, and who does it favor?
flashcards.back_html: A default rule that courts assume the government followed proper procedure and acted in good faith. It favors the government: the challenger must prove irregularity or willful violation.

flashcards.prompt: What is the practical consequence when judges stop extending the presumption?

choices.text: Government lawyers must support factual claims with sworn testimony and evidence rather than representations
The government automatically loses every case it files
Cases are transferred to state court

flashcards.explanation_html: Judges like Christine O'Hearn said they would no longer accept statements of fact unless made under oath — converting an assumption into something that must be proved.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a doctrine like the presumption of regularity necessary in the first place?

choices.text: Courts cannot independently verify every government action, so they need a workable starting assumption
The Constitution explicitly requires deference to executive agencies
It is required by international treaty

flashcards.explanation_html: It is a practical device: without some default, every routine government act would need to be proved from scratch. That is also why losing it is costly for the government.
